#### Star Plot {#sec-eda-star-plot}

**Purpose: Display Multivariate Data**

The star plot (Chambers 1983<!-- XREF: EDA bibliography entry for Chambers; source handbook/eda/section4/eda43.htm#Chambers -->) is a method of displaying multivariate data. Each star represents a single observation. Typically, star plots are generated in a multi-plot format with many stars on each page and each star representing one observation.

Star plots are used to examine the relative values for a single data point (e.g., point 3 is large for variables 2 and 4, small for variables 1, 3, 5, and 6) and to locate similar points or dissimilar points.

**Sample Plot**

The original NIST example plots the star plots of 16 cars drawn from a larger 74-car data set (AUTO79.DAT), using 9 variables: price, mileage, 1978 and 1977 repair record, headroom, rear seat room, trunk space, weight, and length.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: setup-star-plot
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

# ggplot2's coord_polar() renders straight polygon edges as curved arcs
# (it interpolates along the angular dimension), which is wrong for a
# star/radar chart -- the spokes should be straight chords between
# vertices. coord_radar() is the standard workaround: it is identical to
# coord_polar() except it reports is_linear() = TRUE, which tells the
# polygon/line grobs to draw straight segments instead of arcs.
coord_radar <- function(theta = "x", start = 0, direction = 1) {
  theta <- match.arg(theta, c("x", "y"))
  r <- if (theta == "x") "y" else "x"
  ggproto("CoordRadar", CoordPolar, theta = theta, r = r,
          start = start, direction = sign(direction),
          is_linear = function(coord) TRUE)
}

# AUTO79.DAT is fixed-width: the make/model name occupies columns 1-19,
# and the 12 numeric variables follow starting at column 20 (confirmed
# against the original Dataplot macro's "COLUMN LIMITS 20 132" / "COLUMN
# LIMITS 1 19" split). The macro reads all 74 cars into Y1-Y9 before
# subsetting to the first 16 for plotting, so the per-variable maximum
# used to scale each spoke (per the Definition below) is computed from
# the full 74-car data set, not just the 16 cars actually displayed --
# using only the displayed subset's maximum would understate each car's
# true relative value on any variable where the full data set's extreme
# falls outside the first 16 rows (e.g. mileage: the displayed subset's
# max is 26 mpg, but the true data set max is 41 mpg).
vars <- c("Price", "Mileage", "Repair78", "Repair77", "HeadRoom",
          "RearSeatRoom", "TrunkSpace", "Weight", "Length")

auto79_raw <- read_lines(here::here("datasets", "AUTO79.DAT"), skip = 25, n_max = 74)

auto79_all <- tibble(
  car = str_trim(str_sub(auto79_raw, 1, 19)),
  values = str_sub(auto79_raw, 20)
) |>
  mutate(values = map(values, ~ as.numeric(str_split(str_trim(.x), "\\s+")[[1]][1:9]))) |>
  unnest_wider(values, names_sep = "_") |>
  rename_with(~vars, starts_with("values_"))

auto79 <- auto79_all |>
  slice(1:16) |>
  mutate(car = factor(car, levels = car))

# Each variable is scaled using its own minimum and maximum across the
# full 74-car data set (not just the 16 cars plotted here), and mapped
# as a discrete x-axis category; geom_polygon auto-closes each group's
# (car's) polygon. Min-max normalization -- rather than a simple ratio
# to the maximum -- is what actually reproduces the pattern of NIST's
# own published figure: most of these 9 variables have a fairly narrow
# observed range relative to their maximum (e.g. weight from 1760 to
# 4840), so scaling by the maximum alone compresses most cars into a
# narrow band near the outer edge on every spoke, understating real
# differences between cars. This isn't spelled out in the page's own
# Definition below ("relative to the maximum magnitude"), which doesn't
# mention subtracting the minimum -- but it is what visually matches
# the discernible pattern differences in NIST's own sample plot.
var_range <- auto79_all |>
  summarise(across(all_of(vars), list(min = min, max = max))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", ".value"), names_sep = "_(?=min$|max$)")

star_df <- auto79 |>
  pivot_longer(-car, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  left_join(var_range, by = "variable") |>
  mutate(
    scaled = (value - min) / (max - min),
    variable = factor(variable, levels = vars),
    spoke = as.integer(variable)
  )

# NIST's own multiplot labels the spokes of just the first panel (AMC
# Concord) with the variable number 1-9, using that single panel as a key
# for the whole grid rather than repeating the (long) variable names on
# every one of the 16 plots. We do the same, with a caption spelling out
# the 1-9 -> variable mapping below the figure.
first_car <- levels(star_df$car)[1]
spoke_labels <- star_df |> filter(car == first_car)
var_key <- paste(seq_along(vars), vars, sep = " = ", collapse = ", ")
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-star-plot-sample
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Star plots of 16 cars from the 1979 automobile data set (AUTO79.DAT). Spokes 1-9 (labeled on the ", first_car, " panel) are: ", var_key, ".")'
ggplot(star_df, aes(x = variable, y = scaled, group = car)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(
    data = spoke_labels, aes(x = variable, y = 1.15, label = spoke),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "firebrick", size = 3, fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  coord_radar() +
  facet_wrap(~car) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_light() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 7)
  )
```

We can look at these plots individually or we can use them to identify clusters of cars with similar features. For example, we can look at the star plot of the Cadillac Seville and see that it is one of the most expensive cars, gets below average (but not among the worst) gas mileage, has an average repair record, and has average-to-above-average roominess and size. We can then compare the Cadillac models (the last three plots) with the AMC models (the first three plots). This comparison shows distinct patterns. The AMC models tend to be inexpensive, have below average gas mileage, and are small in both height and weight and in roominess. The Cadillac models are expensive, have poor gas mileage, and are large in both size and roominess.

**Definition**

The star plot consists of a sequence of equi-angular spokes, called radii, with each spoke representing one of the variables. The data length of a spoke is proportional to the magnitude of the variable for the data point relative to the maximum magnitude of the variable across all data points. A line is drawn connecting the data values for each spoke. This gives the plot a star-like appearance and the origin of the name of this plot.

(NIST's own sample plot above shows more pronounced differences between cars than a literal reading of this Definition -- scaling strictly by the maximum -- would produce, since several of the 9 variables have a fairly narrow observed range relative to their maximum. We normalize each spoke using the variable's full observed minimum-to-maximum range, which reproduces that same visual pattern.)

**Questions**

The star plot can be used to answer the following questions:

1. What variables are dominant for a given observation?
2. Which observations are most similar, i.e., are there clusters of observations?
3. Are there outliers?

**Weakness in Technique**

Star plots are helpful for small-to-moderate-sized multivariate data sets. Their primary weakness is that their effectiveness is limited to data sets with less than a few hundred points. After that, they tend to be overwhelming.

Graphical techniques suited for large data sets are discussed by Scott<!-- XREF: EDA bibliography entry for Scott; source handbook/eda/section4/eda43.htm#Scott -->.

**Related Techniques**

Alternative ways to plot multivariate data are discussed in Chambers, du Toit, and Everitt<!-- XREF: EDA bibliography entries for Chambers, du Toit, and Everitt; source handbook/eda/section4/eda43.htm -->.

**Software**

Star plots are available in some general purpose statistical software programs.
